We show that these generalized tensor cluster expansion features span a subspace of MACE features, suggesting that TCE features can sufficiently pre-screen MACE features for chemical diversity in alloyed transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers. We show that, using maximum-entropy subset sampling, we can empirically recover chemical diversity from MACE features using a cheaper TCE representation. We then fine-tune a multi-ACE (MACE) potential with both subsets, and use this potential to predict temperature-dependent vibrational properties in alloyed TMD monolayers with varying chemical ordering. In our approach, TCE features can be used as cheap surrogate features for pre-screening chemically rich configurations using MACE features, allowing for the more efficient finetuning of atomic cluster expansion (ACE) potentials, thus achieving a tractable prediction of finite-temperature alloy thermodynamics on modest hardware.

articles.title: Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. I. Clean surface properties
articles.abstract: Ab initio calculations were used to elucidate the properties of the polar surfaces of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors, i.e., metal- and nonmetal-terminated. The systems considered were clean wurtzite gallium nitride (i.e. (0001) and (000-1) GaN surfaces), zinc blende gallium phosphide (i.e. (111) and (-1-1-1) GaP), gallium arsenide (i.e. (111) and (-1-1-1) GaAs), and (111) and (-1-1-1) GaSb surfaces. The calculated data include the crystallographic structure and the electronic states of the termination atoms on both sides, i.e. their positions, energies, and occupations. All nonmetal-terminated surfaces exhibit no reconstruction, and their broken-bond states are located in the vicinity of the valence band maxima (VBM), pinning the Fermi level. The Ga-terminated surface exhibited (4 x 4) reconstruction related to the division of termination atoms into sp3 and sp2 hybridized in proportions of 6 to 10, based on charge redistribution according to the electron counting rule (ECR). Thus, the broken-bond state is separated into two sets, occupied and empty, with the Fermi level located between them in the vicinity of the conduction band minimum (CBM).

articles.title: Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. II. Adsorption of nonmetal atoms (N, P, As, and Sb) on Ga-terminated surfaces
articles.abstract: Ab initio calculations were used to simulate the adsorption processes on Ga-terminated surfaces of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. The considered adsorbates are nonmetal species, i.e., nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony on wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e., GaN(0001) surfaces, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e., GaP(111), gallium arsenide, GaAs(111), and gallium antimonide, GaSb (111) surfaces. The cases investigated include single adsorbed nonmetal atoms and full coverage, i.e. theta=1 of these surfaces. The calculated results include the stable sites and the energies of the single adsorbed atoms: located at H3 sites at low coverage and in on-top positions at high coverage for GaP, GaAs and GaSb. At high nitrogen coverage, the N2 admolecules are formed, weakly attached to the surface. The calculated electronic properties of the single-adatom systems include the band diagrams of the slabs in real and momentum space, the energies of the quantum states. In addition, the overlaps of the quantum states of the nonmetal adatoms and the nearest topmost surface Ga atoms are given. The full coverage data include the atomic configurations and the bond energies of the adsorbed layers. The electronic properties include the above-mentioned data for single adatoms, together with additional properties related to interactions between adsorbed atoms. The evaporation stability analysis confirms that the adatoms stabilize the topmost Ga atoms against detachment because of the high energy barrier of DE > 3 eV which is further increased to DE > 4 eV by coverage located at H3 sites. Thus, growth simulations should employ unreconstructed Ga-terminated surfaces covered by nonmetal atoms located at on-top positions.

articles.title: Y2CdX4 (X = S, Se, Te) Semiconductors: A First-Principles Study of Structural, Electronic, Optical, and Energy-Related Properties
articles.abstract: We present a comprehensive density functional theory (DFT) investigation of the structural, mechanical, electronic, optical, thermoelectric, and bonding properties of Y2CdX4 (X = S, Se, Te) compounds for potential optoelectronic and energy-conversion applications. Structural optimization reveals a systematic expansion of the equilibrium lattice parameters from S to Te. The calculated bulk moduli decrease from 83 GPa for Y2CdS4 to 68 GPa for Y2CdSe4 and 54 GPa for Y2CdTe4, indicating progressive lattice softening. Electronic band-structure calculations predict indirect band gaps of 2.42, 2.08, and 1.71 eV for Y2CdS4, Y2CdSe4, and Y2CdTe4, respectively, with further narrowing upon inclusion of spin-orbit coupling. The calculated dielectric functions, refractive indices, absorption coefficients, reflectivity, optical conductivities, and electron energy-loss spectra reveal systematic changes in optical response across the chalcogen series. The absorption onset shifts toward lower photon energies, from approximately 2.4 eV in Y2CdS4 to 1.7 eV in Y2CdTe4. Thermoelectric calculations indicate promising Seebeck coefficients and power factors, with Y2CdSe4 exhibiting a favorable balance of transport properties. Charge-density distributions, electron localization functions, and Bader charge analyses suggest increasing covalent bonding contributions from sulfide to telluride. These findings highlight the potential of Y2CdX4 compounds for tunable optoelectronic and energy-conversion applications.

articles.title: Compensation of hyperexcitability with simulation-based inference
articles.abstract: The activity of healthy neuronal networks is tightly regulated, and a shift toward hyperexcitability can cause various problems, such as epilepsies, memory deficits, and motor disorders. Numerous cellular, synaptic, and intrinsic mechanisms of hyperexcitability and compensatory mechanisms to restore healthy activity have been proposed. However, quantifying multiple compensatory mechanisms and their dependence on specific pathophysiological mechanisms has proven challenging, even in computational models. We use simulation-based inference to quantify the interactions of putative compensatory mechanisms in a spiking neuronal network model. Various parameters of the model can compensate for the changes in other parameters to maintain baseline activity, and we estimated their compensatory potential. Furthermore, specific causes of hyperexcitability – interneuron loss, excitatory recurrent synapses, and principal cell depolarization – have distinct compensatory mechanisms that can restore normal excitability. Our results show that spiking neuronal network simulators could generate hypotheses about the mechanisms of pathophysiological network mechanisms.

articles.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan
articles.abstract: The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

articles.title: Fitness level, but not sex, affects exercise-induced pain modulation
articles.abstract: In a previous study by our group (Nold et al., 2025), we investigated exercise-induced pain modulation after high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise in a heterogeneous sample of diverse fitness levels. Exploratory analyses suggested an interaction of sex, fitness level, and drug treatment, indicating that males showed increasing hypoalgesia after high- compared to low-intensity exercise with increasing fitness levels, which was diminished when naloxone was administered. In contrast, these effects were not evident in females. These exploratory findings warranted further investigation to determine if and to what extent exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level and/or sex. In this current study, we investigated an all-female sample (N=21) of high fitness levels using a similar paradigm as in the previous study, comparing heat and pressure pain ratings after high-intensity and low-intensity exercise. Our data show an interaction of exercise intensity and stimulus intensity in heat pain, with greater pain relief following high-intensity exercise, especially at the highest stimulus intensity. Despite results for pressure pain not reaching significance, a similar trend was evident. These results suggest that females at a high fitness level also show exercise-induced pain modulation for high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise. Furthermore, we pooled the data of the current and previous study, providing evidence for fitness level but not sex to moderate exercise-induced pain modulation in heat pain. These findings suggest that exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level but not on sex.

articles.title: Glutamate receptor composition at Drosophila neuromuscular junctions depends on developmental stage and muscle identity
articles.abstract: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of larval Drosophila is widely used for studying synaptic transmission. Larval body wall muscles express five ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) subunits that assemble into two tetrameric complexes, with subunit composition determining the strength and plasticity of synaptic transmission. Because NMJ function has been extensively characterized in larvae, it has commonly been assumed that adult fly NMJs share this molecular composition, despite substantial differences between life stages. Here, we systematically compare glutamate receptor expression across larval and adult Drosophila muscles. We find that adult leg and flight muscles exhibit different iGluR expression than larvae, lacking expression of several receptors previously considered essential. Adjacent muscles within the adult femur express distinct iGluRs, suggesting specialization of flexor and extensor muscles. Finally, the glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluClα) is expressed extrasynaptically in adult but not larval muscle fibers. Our results reveal unexpected heterogeneity in glutamate receptor expression across muscles and developmental stages, demonstrating the need for muscle-specific analyses in flies and other animals.

articles.title: Oxytocin neurons signal state-dependent transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal
articles.abstract: Core body temperature (Tb) is defended within narrow limits through thermoregulatory behaviors like huddling, nesting, and physical activity, as well as autonomic responses like brown fat thermogenesis. While Tb displays regulated fluctuations across different behavioral states and rest/arousal cycles, the neural control of these transitions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the relationship between oxytocin neurons of the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVNOT) and behavioral and autonomic thermoeffector pathways across physiological states in mice. First, we show that PVNOT neurons are activated during social thermoregulation. We then demonstrate that in vivo PVNOT calcium dynamics align with transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal. Counter to our initial hypothesis, these dynamics were observed in both social and non-social contexts. Using a computer vision model to track thermoeffector pathways, we demonstrate that precisely timed stimulation of PVNOT neurons during low-Tb resting states increases thermogenesis followed by behavioral arousal. We therefore suggest a model in which PVNOT neurons facilitate homeostatic state-dependent transitions in thermo-behavioral states.

articles.title: SVEP1 enables efficient binding of angiopoietin-2 to the TIE1 receptor, allowing receptor phosphorylation and downstream signaling
articles.abstract: The molecular mechanisms that drive (lymph-)angiogenesis are crucial to understanding diseases, such as lymphedema, that are caused due to malformations of the lymphatic vasculature. Recently, an interaction between the secreted protein Svep1, a key regulator in lymphangiogenesis, and the transmembrane receptor Tie1 was shown in zebrafish, humans, and mice. Here, guided by in silico AlphaFold-multimer structure predictions of SVEP1 complexes, we assert with protein binding studies that the human CCP20 domain is the primary binding site for TIE1. We further demonstrate that SVEP1 mediates strong binding of ANG2 and TIE1, and that combined stimulation of hdLECs with SVEP1 and ANG2 leads to phosphorylation of TIE1. TIE1 activation by SVEP1 and ANG2 enables downstream signaling and, in turn, potentiates nuclear exclusion of FOXO1 and phosphorylation of AKT compared to SVEP1 or ANG2 alone. We present a model in which ANG1/2 dimers bind to both SVEP1 and TIE1, resulting in the recruitment of multiple TIE1 receptor molecules to a multimeric complex at the cell membrane, potentially amplifying its signaling capacity.

articles.title: ARCADE: Automated and Interpretable Design of Complex Catalysts
articles.abstract: The rational design of high-performance catalysts is pivotal for modern industry but is often hindered by the time-consuming nature of trial-and-error methods. While computational and data-driven approaches have accelerated materials discovery, significant challenges remain, especially for complex systems like multielement disordered nanoparticles. These challenges include immense computational costs, difficulties in modeling stability and heterogeneous active sites, and a lack of interpretability in “black-box” AI models. To address these multifaceted challenges, herein, we introduce ARCADE (Automated Rational Catalyst Design), a generalizable and transferable framework for the automated and interpretable design of complex catalysts. This highly cohesive pipeline introduces key methodological innovations in realistic structure generation, autonomous active-site processing, and short-range order guided interpretability, seamlessly coupled with state-of-the-art pH-dependent microkinetic modeling. Notably, ARCADE streamlines the structural modeling of irregular nanoparticles by transforming intractable combinatorial enumeration into a targeted iterative search; robustly identifies active sites and subsequently resolves ubiquitous adsorbate drift issues arising during structural relaxations; and employs geometric short-range order descriptors derived contribution scores to rapidly decode catalytic mechanisms, thereby efficiently unraveling the complex synergistic effects inherent in multielement catalysts. Using the challenging design of multielement nanoparticle catalysts for CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) as a representative system, we demonstrate that ARCADE can systematically navigate the design process, from evaluating material stability to identifying site-specific activity and selectivity. Our results show that this methodology substantially accelerates the development cycle for complex catalysts, confirming its feasibility and broad applicability. Crucially, this work establishes a fully integrated paradigm for the rational design and discovery of complex materials for challenging chemical reactions.

articles.title: Achieving Low-Temperature High-Efficient Ammonia Decomposition Over sub-nm Ru Cluster with CeO2– x Support via Photopromoted Hydrogen Spillover and Nitrogen Recombination
articles.abstract: The low-temperature high-efficient decomposition of ammonia, a carbon-free hydrogen carrier, is essential to the promising hydrogen energy storage. However, the decomposition is hindered by slow reaction kinetics due to dynamically hydrogen poisoning and thermodynamically high nitrogen recombination barrier in ordinary thermocatalysis. Herein, we propose a photothermocatalytic strategy to resolve these kinetic issues and achieve enhanced hydrogen production. Under full-spectrum light irradiance of 20 kW m–2, a hydrogen production rate of 4.2 mmol g–1 min–1 at 300 °C has been achieved over the Ru/CeO2–x catalyst, significantly outperforming conventional thermocatalysis. Insights from in situ characterizations and density functional theory calculations indicate that the enhanced performance is ascribed to photopromoted hydrogen spillover and nitrogen recombination, which are mediated by the strong metal–support interaction. On one hand, the photogenerated electrons promote the H dissociation over sub-nm Ru clusters and migration across the metal–support interface, and the photoinduced oxygen-vacancy-rich CeO2–x surface favors to spread the active H· species. On the other hand, the photogenerated electrons reduce the activation energy for Ru–N bond cleavage, which is beneficial for N–N recombination. This study has demonstrated the distinct advantage of photothermocatalytic hydrogen production as an energy-saving, high-efficient, and carbon-free route.

articles.title: Anionic Photocatalyst as Excited-State Super-Reductants in Organic Synthesis
articles.abstract: Organic chromophores have emerged as powerful photoreductants in modern photocatalysis, enabling a wide range of synthetically valuable transformations under mild conditions. Among these, anionic chromophores constitute a particularly distinctive class owing to their extreme reducing power in the photoexcited state. Deprotonation-driven generation of anionic species frequently induces a bathochromic shift in the absorption profile of the parent neutral chromophore, thereby extending light harvesting into the visible region. More importantly, localization of negative charge on a heteroatom or π-conjugated framework can promote intramolecular charge-transfer transitions when an appropriate electron-accepting motif is present. Such excited states often exhibit prolonged lifetimes, facilitating diffusion-controlled electron transfer with substrates. Collectively, these features endow photoexcited anions with extraordinary reducing power, enabling the activation of some of the most reductively recalcitrant chemical bonds that remain inaccessible to conventional photocatalysts. In recent years, the rapid expansion of anion-mediated photochemistry has established photoexcited anions—many of which are generated in situ—as versatile super-reductants for addressing longstanding challenges in synthetic chemistry. This review highlights the fundamental design principles governing anionic photocatalysts, their photophysical and photochemical properties, and the mechanistic features that underpin their reactivity. We further provide a comprehensive overview of the diverse classes of anionic chromophores and their emerging applications, and discuss future opportunities to advance anion-based organophotocatalysis.

articles.title: Correction to “Boosting Benzene Hydroxylation via Hydroxyl-Migration-Mediated Synergy of Spatially Isolated Cu and La Single Atoms”
Entropy–Enthalpy Compensation in Electrocatalytic Rates
articles.abstract: Measuring the temperature dependence of electrocatalytic reaction rates is a powerful, yet underexplored, way of investigating the underlying kinetics. In this study, we develop the understanding behind such kinetic measurements. Through a very simple model of the surface kinetics for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), we explore how extracted Arrhenius parameters depend on potential and rationalize a series of entropy-enthalpy correlations in experimental HER rates. We find that the entropy-dependent prefactor can change alongside the apparent activation energy, thus signaling deviations from the established Butler-Volmer kinetics that have so far mostly been attributed to potential-driven solvent dynamics. Distinct kinetic fingerprints emerge for different groups of metal catalysts that are in qualitative agreement with recent experiments. We elucidate these characteristic fingerprints in terms of shifting kinetic regimes and generalize our findings to other electrocatalytic reactions and setups. Our analysis overall suggests the entropy loss/gain due to species’ adsorption/desorption as the main driver behind measured changes in the Arrhenius prefactor.

articles.title: Light-Reconfigured Adsorption over Zeolite-Confined Amorphous Multicomponent Alloy Nanoparticles Enables Photothermal Dry Reforming of Methane
articles.abstract: High-temperature dry reforming of methane (DRM) over Ni-based catalysts is limited by sintering and coking, while competitive adsorption can further restrict efficient utilization of CH4 and CO2. Here, we report a one-step hydrothermal strategy to encapsulate amorphous NiCoCuZnMn multicomponent alloy nanoparticles with partially oxidized Zn/Mn-containing surface domains within a TS-1 zeolite matrix, affording a structurally confined photothermal catalyst (denoted MA@TS-1). Under illumination, MA@TS-1 reaches a CO production rate of 21.85 mmol g–1 h–1 at 450 °C and sustains continuous operation for 500 h. Kinetic analysis, pulse-response experiments, in situ DRIFTS, and illumination-dependent XPS collectively show that irradiation changes both the adsorption response and the surface electronic state of the catalyst. CO2 pre-adsorption strongly suppresses subsequent CH4 net retention in the dark, whereas the corresponding CO2-induced pulse-response loss is markedly attenuated under illumination. Concurrently, opposite XPS shifts of Ni and the Zn/Mn-associated species are consistent with illumination-induced interfacial electronic redistribution accompanied by relative electron enrichment of Ni-rich sites. Control catalysts and qualitative DFT calculations further support a model in which CH4 activation preferentially involves Zn/Mn oxide-associated interfacial regions, whereas CO2 activation is favored at Ni-rich sites. These results show that light-responsive electronic and adsorption modulation can accompany photothermal heating and provide a route to regulating competitive adsorption in multicomponent DRM catalysts.

articles.title: Ring-Expansion/Cross-Coupling Cascade of Ketones via Radical Sorting
articles.abstract: Ring-expansion/cross-coupling cascade of saturated carbocycles remains an underdeveloped strategy, despite its immense potential to provide rapid access to molecular architectures that are challenging to synthesize in a single operation. Herein, we report a dual photoredox/nickel catalyzed ring-expansion/cross-coupling cascade of ketones through radical sorting, employing carboxylic acid derivatives as C(sp3) coupling partners. This protocol is broadly applicable to the one-carbon ring-expansion and concomitant functionalization of diverse 5-, 6-, 7-, 8-, 12-, 13-, 14-, and 16-membered ketones using various redox-active esters that bear a wide range of functional groups. Remarkably, the strategy can also be extended to three-carbon ring-expansion, enabling remote functionalization of ketone frameworks. Furthermore, the methodology is applicable to acyclic ketones, enabling a chain-extension/cross-coupling cascade. The synthetic utility of the methodology is demonstrated through late-stage scaffold remodeling of drugs and natural products, as well as the synthesis of 3-methylmuscone. Mechanistic investigations, supported by DFT calculations, shed light on selectivity in the coupling step and provide compelling evidence for a homolytic bimolecular substitution (SH2) pathway.

articles.title: Ruthenium Single Atom Switches the Interfacial Mechanism to Mars–van Krevelen for Coking-Resistant Photothermocatalytic Reforming of (Micro)Plastics with CO2
articles.abstract: Photothermal dry reforming of polyethylene (PE) with carbon dioxide (CO2) is a promising route for waste plastic and greenhouse gas valorization, but mismatched PE cracking and CO2 activation kinetics cause coke deposition and limit reforming stability. Here, we develop a photothermal catalyst, Ru1Cun/TiO2–x, that enables efficient and stable conversion of PE and CO2 into syngas under simulated and natural sunlight across diverse plastic feedstocks. Mechanistic studies show that Ru single atoms reconstruct the Cu-TiO2–x interface, shifting the reaction from a Langmuir–Hinshelwood mechanism to a Mars–van Krevelen (MvK) pathway that strengthens CO2 activation and lattice oxygen cycling, thereby directing PE-derived intermediates through sequential oxidation before dehydrogenation and suppressing coke formation. Life-cycle assessment and scale-up simulations show that solar-driven photothermal co-reforming has a lower carbon footprint than conventional plastic upcycling, supporting its feasibility and scalability for solar-driven plastic waste remediation and greenhouse gas utilization.

articles.title: Visible-Light-Driven Dehydrogenative Ketone Synthesis from Unprotected Primary Alcohols and Aryl Bromides
articles.abstract: Owing to their widespread natural abundance, alcohols are regarded as highly attractive coupling partners in organic synthesis. Although O–H or C–O activating cross-couplings of alcohols have been well-established in distinct contexts, the direct C–H oxidative coupling of alcohols to form ketones remains rare. Herein, we disclose a visible-light-driven, bromine-radical-mediated hydrogen-atom-transfer/nickel relay that enables the direct conversion of unprotected primary alcohols and aryl bromides to aryl alkyl ketones under ambient conditions. The transformation merges selective α-C–H arylation of alcohols with in situ dehydrogenation of the resulting secondary alcohol intermediates, thereby accomplishing C–C bond formation and ketone formation in one catalytic manifold without an exogenous stoichiometric oxidant or hydrogen acceptor. The protocol is compatible with simple and functionalized primary alcohols, aryl and heteroaryl bromides, as well as complex fragments relevant to late-stage diversification, delivering 80 ketone products in up to 91% yield. Combined mechanistic experiments and density functional theory calculations support a pathway initiated by bromine-radical-mediated hydrogen-atom transfer to generate ketyl radicals, followed by nickel-catalyzed arylation and dehydrogenation of the resulting secondary alcohol intermediates to furnish the ketone products. This work establishes native primary alcohols as practical ketone-building partners in metallaphotoredox catalysis and offers a mild and efficient cross-coupling strategy for the direct transformation of alcohols to ketones.

articles.title: Predictive Design Principles for Plasma-Catalysis
articles.abstract: Centralized production of fuels and commodity chemicals emits 1.4–2 Gt CO2 yr–1 and depends on fossil-fuel supply chains that prevent distributed deployment. Nonthermal plasmas offer a path to decentralized, electrified production by generating vibrationally excited molecules, radicals, and ions without bulk heating of gas. Despite this potential, plasma-catalysis remains difficult to design because plasma excitation, surface reaction energetics, and intermediate removal are treated separately, and activity trends do not transfer across chemistries. This perspective develops a quantitative framework connecting nonequilibrium excitation, surface binding energetics, coreactant chemistry, and surface temperature to reaction rates, selectivity, and catalyst stability. Reactions are classified into three kinetic regimes by the balance between intermediate supply and removal rates, each with distinct rate-controlling steps and deactivation modes. Design tools and principles derived from this classification are applied to four example case studies that transfer across chemistries without reparameterization and provide a basis for reactor design at scale.

articles.title: Carrier-Induced and Coherent-Phonon-Controlled Band Renormalization in Quasi-One-Dimensional α-Bi4Br4
articles.abstract: Directional control of band structures at ultrafast time scales is a key requirement for nanoscale optoelectronics. Here, we realize cooperative band engineering in the quasi-one-dimensional (quasi-1D) van der Waals topological insulator α-Bi4Br4 through joint carrier-phonon band renormalization. Femtosecond excitation drives quasi-1D carrier accumulation, generating a strongly nonlinear many-body band renormalization that redshifts an optical transition by up to ∼25 meV, with >90% polarization anisotropy. Superimposed Ag coherent phonons further modulate the same transition by ∼1 meV on intrinsic lattice time scales. By implementing phase-controlled dual-pump excitation, we achieve deterministic and reversible positioning of the renormalized band edge with ∼100 μeV precision within a ∼1.5 meV tuning window. First-principles calculations with charge-neutral photoexcitation constraints qualitatively reproduce the carrier-induced narrowing of the relevant interband transition, while phonon-mode analysis reveals that coherent Ag phonons modulate the same transition through interchain hopping and orbital polarization. These results establish cooperative carrier-phonon band renormalization as a scalable, all-optical mechanism for ultrafast, polarization-sensitive band engineering in quasi-1D van der Waals nanomaterials, enabling dynamically reconfigurable optoelectronic functionality.

articles.title: Colloidal Atomic Layer Deposition on Plasmonic Metal Oxide Nanocrystals
articles.abstract: Colloidal atomic layer deposition (c-ALD) has emerged as a powerful technique for enhancing the functional properties of nanocrystals (NCs) while preserving their solution dispersibility. Previous studies have shown that the deposition of amorphous metal oxide shells via c-ALD can passivate surface states in NCs, resulting in improved stability, photoluminescence, conductivity, and energy transfer. However, its application to doped metal oxide NCs, such as tin-doped indium oxide (ITO), which exhibit surface depletion due to surface hydroxyls, remains unexplored. In this work, we implement a c-ALD strategy using ligand-modified precursors to grow amorphous Al2O3, TiO2, and Ga2O3 shells on ITO NCs. We reveal how these coatings influence the plasmonic response and mitigate surface depletion, which we ascribe to surface state passivation. Energy-dependent X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) reveals a reduction in band bending, indicating a modification of the near-surface electronic structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that control over shell thickness enables tunability of the collective plasmonic resonances in assembled ITO NC superlattices. This work expands the scope of c-ALD and establishes a versatile approach for tailoring the optoelectronic properties of doped metal oxide NCs in solution-processable systems.

articles.title: Halide Exchange Reactions in Large Halide Perovskite Nanocrystals
articles.abstract: We have studied halide exchange reactions in large colloidal nanocrystals of lead halide perovskites, with sizes (∼40–60 nm) that are intermediate between those of typical nanocrystals synthesized and studied by the community (5–10 nm) and those of microcrystals or thin films. This size regime still allows an investigation of the nanocrystals with techniques used for colloidal nanocrystals while enabling the observation of phenomena such as phase segregation, generation of planar defects, strain accumulation and relaxation, which are harder to identify in smaller nanocrystals, also given their high instability under the electron beam. We compare nanocubes with hollow nanocubes, and highlight how the presence of the hollow region can influence structural and morphological changes during the reactions. Notably, we report core–shell epitaxial CsPbI3/CsPbCl3 heterostructures by partial I– to Cl– exchange on CsPbI3 nanocrystals. Transient absorption spectroscopy provides evidence consistent with electronic coupling and exciton transfer between the Cl-rich shell and I-rich core in these heterostructures, evidenced by the accelerated bleach decay of the CsPbCl3 component and the delayed population of the CsPbI3 band edge.

articles.title: Highly Emissive NIR-II Unimolecular Micelles via a Core–Cap Synthetic Strategy for Deep-Tissue Imaging and Image-Guided Surgery
articles.abstract: High-performance fluorescence imaging in the second near-infrared (NIR-II, 1000–1700 nm) window holds promise for deep-tissue optical diagnostics. However, simultaneously achieving high fluorescence quantum yields (QYs) and ultrasmall dimensions in physiological aqueous environments remains a fundamental challenge. Here, we report a de novo core–cap synthetic strategy to construct highly emissive, renal-clearable NIR-II fluorophores based on a unimolecular micelle architecture. By integrating a rigid, donor–acceptor–donor (D–A–D) hydrophobic core containing orthogonal axial and lateral steric shielding networks with a hydrophilic polyethylene glycol (PEG) outer cap, we successfully suppress water-induced nonradiative decay and intermolecular aggregation-induced quenching without compromising lateral conjugation. Molecular dynamics simulations and experimental characterizations reveal that these amphiphilic structures self-assemble into highly monodisperse unimolecular micelles featuring an ultrasmall hydrodynamic diameter of ∼5 nm. The optimized fluorophore exhibits a peak NIR-II emission centered at 1034 nm with a high aqueous QY of 4.6%. Owing to their sub-5 nm dimensions, unimolecular micelles undergo dual renal and hepatic clearance pathways, circumventing the biosafety concerns of prolonged tissue retention typical of conventional nanoparticles. Capitalizing on their high brightness, we demonstrate high-resolution, contrast-enhanced in vivo imaging of systemic and cerebral vasculatures, allowing the quantitative morphometric visualization of structural abnormalities in transgenic brain tumors. Furthermore, these fluorophores enable high-contrast, intraoperative fluorescence-guided tumor resection with clearly defined margins. This work provides a promising strategy for the rational design of bright, fast-clearing organic NIR-II probes for advanced biomedical diagnostics.

articles.title: Morphology-Tunable Nanoparticles of Aspartic Acid Paclitaxel Conjugates for Breast Cancer Treatment
articles.abstract: The structural morphologies of nanomaterials serve as vital determinants in their biological interactions and efficacy in vivo. Achieving programmable control over the assembly morphology solely through molecular design remains challenging. Herein, a supramolecular strategy to control the assembly morphology of prodrugs for the orchestration of drug delivery in vivo is reported. A paclitaxel prodrug (PCA) was synthesized by conjugating aspartic acid with paclitaxel through a succinyl linker. PCA can spontaneously self-assemble into nanofibers. Incorporating the diacylphosphatidylethanolamine-PEG2k (DSPE-PEG2k) induces a morphological transition from fibers to rods and ultimately to spheres. Molecular dynamics simulations show that intermolecular hydrogen bonds fall from approximately 50 in DP1 NFs to fewer than 5 in DP3 NPs, and carboxyl-related atoms in aspartic acid account for 53.24% of the total hydrogen bonds, proving that the carboxyl-mediated hydrogen-bond network dominates anisotropic assembly. Although fibrous and spherical assemblies exhibit the fastest release rate and optimized cellular delivery of paclitaxel in vitro, respectively, the rod-shaped assemblies achieve an optimal combination of prolonged blood circulation, enhanced tumor accumulation, and facilitated cellular internalization, resulting in superior antitumor efficacy in vivo, compared to fibrous and spherical counterparts and Abraxane. This study elucidates how supramolecular interactions regulate the macroscopic morphology of prodrug assemblies at the molecular level, establishing a design paradigm for engineering anisotropic nanomedicines with tailored in vivo fate.

articles.title: NanoBlocks: Creating Genetically Encoded Protein Switches Using Competitive Binding
articles.abstract: Many regulatory mechanisms function by changing a molecule’s conformation such that it is switched between active and inactive states. Engineering macromolecules such as proteins to show robust conformational changes in response to arbitrary, well-defined molecular stimuli is of great interest in fields such as synthetic biology and nanoscale engineering, because it allows the development of “smart” molecular tools. We present a strategy that can convert “simple” affinity binders such as nanobodies into protein switches that undergo clear structural rearrangements in response to their innate targets, by introducing a peptide that competes for the binding site. We demonstrate proof-of-concept implementations of this “NanoBlock” design by developing genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors based on two entirely different binder frameworks, the ALFA nanobody and the PDZ domain of Erbin. We show that our design allows the construction of well-performing protein switches that can reliably detect their targets in vitro, in mammalian cells, as part of fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) experiments, and that also generalizes to the creation of stimulus-responsive enzymes via the integration of a bioluminescent readout. We furthermore develop a theoretical model that rationalizes the observations and provides insight into the underlying molecular mechanisms. Overall, our strategy expands the possibilities to create “smart” protein-based molecules and effectors.

articles.title: Proximity-Induced Charge Transfer, Strain, and Possible Magnetic Exchange in Graphene/CrSBr Heterostructure
articles.abstract: Stacking van der Waals materials provides a powerful route to engineer emergent electronic and magnetic behaviors through proximity-driven interactions. The graphene/CrSBr heterostructure has emerged as a compelling platform in this frontier, exhibiting exotic macroscopic responses (including uniaxial surface-plasmon-polariton propagation and an unconventional quantum Hall effect) indicative of strong interfacial electronic and magnetic coupling. However, a microscopic electronic landscape governing these phenomena has remained elusive. Here, we provide a comprehensive spectroscopic characterization of the graphene/CrSBr interface using a combination of angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), low-energy electron microscopy (LEEM), and density functional theory. We resolve a massive redistribution of interfacial charge that concurrently hole-dopes graphene and populates the quasi-one-dimensional spin-polarized conduction band of CrSBr, leading to interfacial metallization. Furthermore, electronic structure of CrSBr exhibits strong momentum-dependent renormalization distinct from conventional charge doping, and theoretical modeling supported by Raman spectroscopy points to additional interfacial compressive strain. In addition, ARPES reveals a splitting-like feature in the graphene Dirac cone consistent with spin degeneracy lifting, providing possible evidence of magnetic proximity coupling. These findings provide crucial microscopic insight into the system’s optical and transport responses and establish graphene/CrSBr as a versatile platform for charge-transfer control, strain-driven band engineering, magnetic-proximity coupling, and directionally confined excitations for next-generation spintronic and nanophotonic devices.

articles.title: Single-Atom-Mediated Two-Dimensional Heterointerface Stabilizing 1T-MoS2 for Durable Hydrogen Evolution
articles.abstract: The metallic 1T phase of MoS2 provides basal-plane activity and high conductivity that are absent in the semiconducting 2H polymorph, making it attractive for applications in electrocatalysis and energy conversion. However, its intrinsic metastability readily drives relaxation to the 2H ground state, and previous attempts to stabilize 1T-MoS2 have yielded only transient domains or localized perturbations without durable phase retention. Here we show that confining Pt single-atoms (SAs) at the MoS2–graphene heterointerface promotes enhanced stabilization and improved retention of 1T-associated MoS2 signatures, while simultaneously stabilizing the SAs themselves. The interfacial Pt SAs act as atomic-scale anchors, simultaneously redistributing charge and reshaping local coordination to favor the metallic 1T-associated configuration of MoS2. Spectroscopic analyses confirm persistent 1T signatures, and ex situ characterization after operation verifies reliable retention of 1T-MoS2. Density functional theory calculations further corroborate these findings, demonstrating that Pt incorporation reverses the intrinsic phase preference and energetically favors the 1T configuration. Electrochemical measurements further demonstrate nearly unchanged hydrogen evolution activity after 30,000 cycles. Together, these results establish SA-mediated heterointerface engineering as a powerful route to stabilize metastable electronic phases and unlock the full potential of layered materials for energy and electronic technologies.

articles.title: Structure-Affinity Correlations and Separable Optical Activity in Carbon Nanotube Protein Coronas
articles.abstract: Biomolecular corona on nanoparticle surfaces enriches low-abundance proteins and compresses the dynamic range of the plasma proteome. Single-walled carbon nanotubes are particularly attractive because their surface chemistry is highly tunable, and their near-infrared fluorescence directly reports corona modulation. However, how surface chemistry shapes the corona and how the corona relates to the fluorescence response remain unclear. We profiled protein enrichment patterns and the resulting fluorescence in a library of 25 chemically modified carbon nanotubes by quantitative proteomics and near-infrared fluorescence spectroscopy. We found that polymer and quantum-defect chemistry orthogonally modulate corona composition, and protein flexibility and solvent exposure are the most significant factors of enrichment, consistent with dispersion-driven, contact-maximizing interactions. Proteomics and fluorescence correlation analyses indicate that enrichment and fluorescence response are partially decoupled. A subset of corona proteins stays optically silent, but where responses occur, enriched proteins respond at lower, physiologically relevant ranges than depleted ones. Our findings inform design principles for carbon nanomaterial-based sensors and biomarker discovery platforms.

articles.title: Sulfur-Induced Lattice Disordering in Halide Electrolytes Enables Superionic Sodium-Ion Conduction
articles.abstract: Amorphous solid electrolytes provide a promising route to overcoming the ion-transport limitations of crystalline halide frameworks, yet achieving superionic Na+ conduction remains challenging. Herein, we report a mixed-anion amorphous Na-ion solid-state electrolyte, TaCl5-0.5Na2S (NTSC), synthesized via high-energy ball-milling, which exhibits an ultrahigh room-temperature ionic conductivity of 2.9 mS/cm and a low activation energy of 0.276 eV. Structural analyses reveal a highly disordered framework composed of Ta-centered bipolyhedra interconnected via corner-sharing sulfur atoms [Ta2Cl10S], [TaCl5S], [TaCl4S], and [TaCl4S2], evidenced by comprehensive characterizations, forming a flexible, disordered amorphous network. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations identify continuous Na+-diffusion pathways with low migration barriers. Complementary topological analyses further indicate that sulfur incorporation leads to local lattice distortions, shortens Na–Na hopping distances, and enhances framework flexibility, collectively enabling fast, multidimensional Na+ transport. When applied in all-solid-state sodium-ion batteries (ASSNIBs), NTSC enables high reversible capacity (111.95 mAh/g with a Coulombic efficiency of 92.6% at 0.1 C) and excellent cycling stability (76.9% initial capacity retention after 200 cycles at 0.2 C) at room temperature. This work establishes mixed-anion amorphization as an effective design strategy for high-performance Na-ion solid electrolytes.

articles.title: Twist-Tunable Interlayer Excitons in Anisotropic ReS 2 /ReSe 2 Heterostructures
articles.abstract: Interlayer excitons (IEs) in van der Waals heterostructures offer tunable excitonic states with long lifetimes and permanent dipole moments. Prior studies focused on isotropic 2H-phase transition metal dichalcogenides, where bright IE emission is confined near high-symmetry twist angles (0° and 60°), restricting tunability. Here, heterobilayers of monolayer ReS2 and ReSe2, both in the 1T′ phase, exhibit robust polarized IE emission near 1.2 eV across the full twist-angle range (1°–88°), reflecting a hybridization landscape governed by lattice anisotropy rather than valley alignment. The lowest-energy IE transition exhibits a nonmonotonic twist-angle dependence with a total modulation range of ∼60 meV, consistent with moiré-driven band renormalization and modulation of interlayer coupling revealed by first-principles calculations and low-frequency Raman spectroscopy, respectively. Overall IE energy tunability extends to ∼100 meV with multilayer ReS2 and excitation energy variation. These results establish ReS2/ReSe2 as a versatile infrared IE platform enabling polarization-resolved emitters and detectors beyond 2H-symmetry constraints.

articles.title: Aberrant lattice expansion in shock-compressed titanium diboride
Beyond Vegard’s Law: Short-Range Structural Heterogeneity in Gd₂O₃–UO₂ Fuel and Its Impact on Thermophysical Properties
Effect of coherency stress on spinodal decomposition in nanoscale particles
Gradient interface-mediated amorphization of a topologically close-packed phase alters dislocation storage and strain accommodation in a high-entropy alloy
Microstructure evolution during rapid solidification of hypoeutectic Al-Ag alloys near absolute stability
Synergistic modification of single-crystal Li-rich Mn-based cathodes via dual engineering of in-situ LiMgBO3 coating and oxygen vacancies for high-rate capability
Diagnosing the Role of Mn Additives in Aqueous Zn/MnO2 Batteries
articles.abstract: Manganese dioxides are pervasive as cathode materials for aqueous zinc‐ion batteries; however, their energy storage mechanism has proven to be complex. Increasing evidence suggests that Mn dissolution contributes to cathode capacity via a reversible dissolution‐redeposition process, in addition to capacity from Zn2+/H+ (de)intercalation. Understanding the role played by Mn2+ in the electrolyte, particularly when introduced as an electrolyte additive, is important for diagnosing cathode degradation. Using operando X‐ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy, we track Mn2+ in operating cells to gain insights into the complexity of the MnO2 cathode. While some suppression of cathode dissolution by the additive cannot be excluded, our measurements suggest that Mn2+ electrolyte additives improve cycling performance by supplying extra redox‐active Mn during charge, rather than solely by suppressing Mn dissolution, thereby compensating for cathode degradation. Benefiting from operando XRF, we propose that a potential contributor to capacity fading is the incomplete dissolution of the MnO2 cathode and incomplete redeposition of Mn2+ from the electrolyte, and that this fading does not appear to be mitigated by using Mn2+ additives. These findings underscore the necessity of directly tracking Mn2+ evolution, and that improving reversibility requires addressing both the dissolution of MnO2 and the redeposition of Mn2+.

articles.title: High‐Density Energy Storage in Si‐Integrated Dielectric Multilayers Through Interfacial Polarization and ML‐Guided Structural Optimization
articles.abstract: Epitaxial dielectric thin films have attracted considerable attention for better energy storage performance than bulks and polymers, yet their reported recoverable energy density (W rec) commonly excludes the substrate, which limits its relevance to practical device-level energy storage. Here, we develop a Si-integrated BZT//S-BZT multilayer capacitor to address this issue and simultaneously enhance polarization and breakdown strength (E b). By directly integrating the oxide multilayer on Si-based substrates, the contribution of the substrate to the effective device volume is substantially reduced, enabling a realistic energy density (W rec-real) of 105.51 J/cm3, exceeding that of the overwhelming majority of comparable systems. The BZT and S-BZT sublayers exhibit small lattice mismatch but pronounced dielectric contrast, which induces strong interfacial polarization (P inter) without introducing interfacial structural perturbation. Landau–Ginzburg–Devonshire theory and phase-field simulations consistently verify the interface-induced polarization enhancement and agree well with the experimental observations. To further improve Eb , machine learning was employed to establish the relationship between the multilayer structural parameters and E b and to identify the optimal starting-layer thickness. Experimental results closely reproduce the predicted trend, leading to an optimized Big-Mac-n architecture with a high W rec of 131.21 J/cm3 and an Eb of 6.5 MV/cm. The multilayer also exhibits excellent fatigue, frequency, and temperature stability, together with ultrafast discharge capability. This work establishes a data-driven interface-engineering strategy for reliable, Si-integrated dielectric energy-storage capacitors.

articles.title: Operando Mapping of Population Phase Separation and Lithium‐Plating Dynamics in Graphite Electrode Using Optical Microscopy and Microstructure Modeling
articles.abstract: The fast‐charging capability of phase‐separating graphite electrodes is largely constrained by heterogeneous reaction kinetics and sluggish mass transport at both the particle and electrode scales, which increase the risk of parasitic lithium plating and associated safety concerns. A deeper mechanistic understanding of the interplay among phase‐separation dynamics, electrode microstructure, and lithium‐plating propensity is therefore essential for guiding the rational design of advanced electrode architectures and fast‐charging protocols. Here, we combine operando optical microscopy with three‐dimensional microstructure‐resolved phase‐field modeling to resolve the interplay between phase separation and lithium plating. Microscopy captures stages evolution, phase mode transitions and structural dynamics across the particle population and at the single‐particle level, which is driven by the slow interfacial reactions. Non‐equilibrium phase‐field simulations elucidate the kinetic control mechanisms governing phase transitions as the current varies. Importantly, a new mechanism of lithium plating associated with interfacial ohmic resistance is identified. Based on these insights, we evaluate particle‐size‐distribution design and use thermal activation as a mechanistic probe to resolve how temperature alters phase‐separation pathways and lithium‐plating behavior. These results may serve as a foundation for improving the physical understanding and driving optimization of fast charging protocols for lithium‐ion batteries.

articles.title: A Magnetic Robotic Platform for Enhanced Stem‐Cell‐Based Tendon Repair
articles.abstract: Robotics enables regenerative medicine to be more precise, less invasive, and more targeted. Mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) therapy shows great potential for tissue regeneration, but challenges such as low cell survival and limited differentiation ability after in vivo implantation hinder its clinical translation. In this study, we propose a magnetic robotic platform capable of autonomously recognizing and targeting injury sites, as well as delivering noninvasive magnetic stimuli to programmatically regulate MSC functions for tendon repair. This platform integrates 3D‐MRI with real‐time recognition to enable spatial perception of deep tissues, which is visualized through panoramic simulation. It provides an engineering‐precise and intelligent automated magnetic stimulation for the diverse tendon injuries scenarios. We identified pulse electromagnetic field (PEMF) parameters that induced proliferation and tenogenesis of MSCs, respectively, and demonstrated the feasibility of programmed PEMF to sequentially regulate cell behaviors of transplanted MSCs, which contributed to the structure and functional recovery of rat injured tendons. Furthermore, we elucidated the underlying molecular mechanisms by which different magnetic stimuli regulate MSC functions, providing insight into PEMF‐mediated MSCs responses. Generally, this magnetic robotic system offers a noninvasive, precise, and biosafe strategy to enhance MSC‐based therapies, with significant implications for clinical applications and broader regenerative medicine.

articles.title: Biointerface‐Customized Nanomodulators Induce Mitochondria‐Specific Dysfunction to Reprogram Tumor Immunity
articles.abstract: Tumor mitochondria regulate cancer progression and immune evasion. However, current therapeutic strategies lack the subcellular precision required to selectively induce immune‐beneficial mitochondrial dysfunction without causing systemic toxicity. Here, we report a biointerface‐customized nanomodulator (C/C‐HP@M2M‐TPP), developed through a biointerface‐engineered strategy (BES), that integrates sequential targeting and controlled activation to induce mitochondria‐specific dysfunction and reprogram tumor immunity. Through a customized biointerface coating, the nanomodulators achieve preferential tumor accumulation and mitochondria‐directed subcellular localization. Co‐delivered calcium ion donors and efflux inhibitors cooperatively induce mitochondrial ion interference and dysfunction, which is further amplified by photothermal activation. This localized mitochondrial interference promotes immunogenic cell death and robust antitumor immune activation, resulting in potent tumor regression in mice. Integrated single‐cell transcriptomic and proteomic analyses further identify mitochondrial disruption as a key mechanistic driver of tumor immune reprogramming. This work establishes biointerface‐customized nanomodulation as a subcellular immunomodulatory therapeutic strategy in vivo.

articles.title: Dual Neuromodulation Remodels Neuro–Immune Crosstalk and Chemokine Network for Combating Postoperative Progression of Prostate Cancer
articles.abstract: The autonomic nerves drive prostate cancer (PCa) progression, yet a strategy for dual modulation of sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves remains undeveloped. Here, building on the multicenter clinical findings, we develop a personalized nanotechnology‐enabled dual neurotherapy (denoted as ADNT) for PCa. The ADNT employs hybrid nanovesicles composed of autologous tumor cell membranes and functionalized liposomes to codeliver the β‐blocker and the muscarinic receptor antagonist to autonomic nerves in residual tumor. In refractory, highly invasive, and orthotopic murine PCa models, the ADNT effectively delays postoperative recurrence and metastasis. Light‐sheet fluorescence microscopy visually confirms the downregulation of autonomic nerve infiltration. Cytometry by time‐of‐flight reveals that ADNT remodels neuro–immune crosstalk and the chemokine network, promoting antitumor immune response and suppressing tumor progression. Additionally, ADNT also alleviates cancer‐associated cachexia and anxiety. Combined with immune checkpoint blockade, ADNT induces complete responses in 100% of mice. Immunofluorescence staining of human PCa specimens confirms the clinical translatability of ADNT, establishing ADNT as a promising therapeutic strategy for PCa.

articles.title: Entropy Stabilized Li‐Rich Layered Oxide Nanoparticles for Advanced High‐Voltage Cathodes
articles.abstract: The performance enhancement of emerging flexible batteries relies on the development of advanced small‐particle electrode materials. However, current cathode materials with reduced particle size mostly suffer from low operating voltage, especially aqueous based electrodes. In this study, by using laser‐induced carbothermal method, we successfully fabricated high‐entropy doped Li‐rich nanoparticles as layered oxide cathodes that exhibit outstanding high‐voltage performances. The direct bottom–up nanocrystal growth enables the formation of such exclusive Li‐rich nanoparticles with unprecedentedly small diameter of 83.08 nm. As confirmed by atomic‐resolution imaging, operando x‐ray diffraction and synchrotron techniques analysis, the cathode achieves high lattice stability at elevated cut‐off voltage through the combined effects of heteroatomic composition and reduced particle diameters. Molecular dynamics simulations using machine‐learning interatomic potentials further demonstrate suppressed oxygen loss and stabilized transition‐metal framework in the high‐entropy doped cathodes. Consequently, the cathode operates steadily at voltage window of 2.5–4.8 V with ultrahigh power density of 877.9 Wh kg−1 at 1 C. The assembled full cell and fiber battery provide significant practical feasibility during high‐voltage cycling. This work provides an efficient strategy for designing high‐voltage flexible batteries, offering critical insights for next‐generation energy storage research.

articles.title: Fundamental Inhibition of Polyiodide Formation by a Site‐Separated Binder for Highly Stable Aqueous Zinc–Iodine Batteries
articles.abstract: Aqueous Zn–I2 batteries are promising for sustainable energy storage systems, yet their practical performance is severely limited by the formation and shuttling of polyiodide intermediates. Here, we report a site separation strategy to block the generation paths of polyiodides and address the related issues from the source. This is realized with a site‐separated polymer (SSP) binder that strongly and selectively confines I2 and I− at varied functional groups on different side chains. It disrupts their coupling to generate polyiodides chemically. Meanwhile, these effective interactions regulate the thermodynamic features of iodine species, which disfavors the formation of polyiodide intermediates and promotes direct I2/I− conversion during electrochemical reactions. The binder also reinforces cathode integrity at different iodine loadings. Therefore, the I2/SSP cathode delivers 212 mAh g−1 capacity at 0.2 A g−1 and retains 102 mAh g−1 at 50 A g−1, superior to 172 mAh g−1/11 mAh g−1 with the conventional polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder. I2/SSP also realizes 97.1% capacity retention over 31000 cycles at 20 A g−1, again far exceeding 46.8% after 20000 cycles for I2/PVDF. Under a high iodine loading of 50 mg cm−2, the I2/SSP cathode further achieves 10.1 mAh cm−2 capacity with 97.9% retention over 400 cycles.

articles.title: In‐Situ Self‐Evolving µ‐Sn10Bi Cross‐Interlocked Structure and Three‐in‐One Kinetic Enhancement Mechanism: Superb Room/Low‐Temperature Sodium Storage Performance
articles.abstract: Sn with a high theoretical capacity and a low‐voltage plateau is considered a promising anode material for high‐energy‐density sodium ion batteries (HSIBs). However, the huge volume changes and poor conductivity of its sodiation products make it difficult to achieve long‐term stability and excellent rate performance. Herein, a remarkably simple structural reinforcement and three‐in‐one kinetic enhancement strategy is proposed for microsized Sn (µ‐Sn) electrode by introducing trace µ‐Bi. Interestingly, µ‐Bi spontaneously evolves into a 3D cross‐linked interlocked nanosheet network during cycling, ensuring long‐term structural stability of µ‐Sn. Meanwhile, the diametrically opposed patterns of electrical conductivity change in Bi and Sn during sodiation are utilized to achieve dynamic complementarity of their conductivity and reaction kinetics throughout the entire charge/discharge process. Additionally, the supercontinuous (104) crystal plane in the 3D Bi network and the Bi/Sn heterointerface in‐situ formed further accelerate e−/Na+ transfer. As a result, the prepared µ‐Sn10Bi simultaneously exhibits high reversible capacity, excellent rate performance and ultralong cycle life in both half and full cell at room/low temperatures. Structural evolution/kinetic enhancement/sodium storage mechanism and structure‐activity relationship of µ‐Sn10Bi are revealed in detail, providing a constructive view for designing low‐cost, high‐capacity, structurally stable, fast‐charging anode with wide‐temperature adaptability for HSIBs.

articles.title: Ionic‐Ligand‐Assisted Transport in Fluorinated Poly(ionic liquid) Electrolytes Enables 515 Wh Kg−1 Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries
articles.abstract: Decoupling ionic conductivity from polymer segmental relaxation while maintaining interfacial stability remains a pivotal challenge for solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs). In this study, we construct an ionic‐ligand‐assisted transport framework by copolymerizing a fluorinated acrylate polymer with a poly(ionic liquid) (PIL) and optimizing the lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) salt concentration. Density functional theory and molecular dynamics simulations reveal that cationic PIL moieties strongly anchor FSI− anions, creating anion‐rich, spatially correlated coordination pathways that facilitate efficient Li+ hopping. The optimized electrolyte exhibits a high ionic conductivity (0.38 mS cm−1) and an exceptional Li+ transference number (0.77) at 30°C. The fluorinated backbone and PIL synergistically expand the oxidative stability window to 4.94 V and promote an inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on the Li‐metal anode. Consequently, Li||Cu cells cycle stably for over 400 cycles with 99.1% average Coulombic efficiency. Solid‐state Li||LiNi0.9Co0.05Mn0.05O2 (NCM90) cells retain ≈81.0% capacity after 600 cycles at 4.3 V, and ≈83.1% capacity after 200 cycles at 4.5 V. Moreover, a high‐energy‐density (515 Wh kg−1) solid‐state pouch cell with an ultrathin Li anode (50 µm) and a high‐loading NCM90 cathode (≈56 mg cm−2) delivers stable cycling and exceptional safety. This ionic‐ligand regulation paradigm provides critical mechanistic insights for designing high‐performance and high‐safety solid‐state batteries.

articles.title: Ion‐Electron Convergent Interphases Enable Ultrahigh Sulfur Utilization for All‐Solid‐State Li–S Batteries
articles.abstract: All‐solid‐state batteries offer a safer route toward electrochemical energy storage with high energy density, but the active‐material utilization is commonly limited by unbalanced carrier transport dynamics through spatially decoupled delivery pathways, which overlap only at restricted reaction fronts. Such an issue is particularly severe for electronically and ionically insulating sulfur/Li2S, making efficient sulfur conversion the key bottleneck for practical all‐solid‐state lithium–sulfur batteries (ASSLSBs). Here, we propose surface‐bound ion‐electron convergent interphases on the Li2S surface that reconstruct localized triple‐phase contacts into an integrated active surface. Using the effective magnetic moment, originating from spin asymmetry, as a screening criterion for interfacial affinity, Li2FeS2 is identified to form a robust surface‐bound interphase with Li2S, which bridges separated ion and electron pathways at the reaction areas, decreasing the transport tortuosity and lowering the activation barriers for both Li2S oxidation and reduction. Consequently, ASSLSBs stably work over 10 000 cycles at 1 mg cm−2 while delivering a loading‐insensitive sulfur utilization of 97.8% and 95.8% at 1 and 8 mg cm−2, respectively. Moreover, a record areal capacity of 38.69 mAh cm−2 is achieved, highlighting the spatially surface‐bound mixed conductors as an effective design principle for synchronizing coupled ion‐electron transfer (CIET) in all‐solid‐state batteries.

articles.title: Life‐Cycle‐Sustainable Capacitive Deionization Enabled by Organic Molecular Engineering for Selective Ammonium Capture
articles.abstract: Selective ammonium (NH4 +) recovery from complex wastewater streams remains a pivotal challenge in sustainable nitrogen management. Capacitive deionization (CDI) offers an energy-efficient electrochemical route for ion separation, yet its practical application is constrained by the inherent trade-off between NH4 + adsorption capacity and selectivity. Herein, we circumvent this fundamental limitation through the rational molecular engineering of an organic electroactive material, 1,4-bis(1H-imidazo[4,5-b]phenazin-2-yl)benzene (IPB), which features extended electron delocalization and abundant C═N moieties for NH4 +-specific redox-coupled capture. The resulting IPB-based CDI prototype delivers a high NH4 + adsorption capacity of 267.23 mg g−1 and a fast rate of 62.51 mg g−1 min−1, while sustaining remarkable selectivity in complex multi-ion matrices, thereby effectively surpassing the conventional capacity-selectivity trade-off. Notably, CDI adsorption reduces wastewater NH4 + levels to below 3 mg L−1 and achieves 82.3% direct recovery as liquid fertilizer during CDI desorption, as demonstrated by isotope tracing experiments. The CDI process exhibits a low carbon footprint of only 4.66 × 10−2 t CO2-equivalent per tonne of NH4 + treated, underscoring its superior life-cycle sustainability. Therefore, this work proposes a molecularly engineered organic electrode material for high-performance wastewater remediation and circular nutrient recovery, paving the way toward carbon-neutral electrochemical water treatment technologies.

articles.title: Nb5+‐Induced‐CeO2 Lattice Strain for Robust and Scalable Solar‐Driven Ammonia Synthesis
articles.abstract: Ammonia (NH3) underpins fertilizer production and is emerging as a renewable-energy carrier. Solar-driven gas-phase N2/H2 conversion requires catalysts that couple efficient light utilization with structural stability under H2-rich conditions. Here, Nb5+ incorporation into CeO2 contracts the lattice and induces compressive microstrain, suppressing excessive oxygen-sublattice reduction and preserving Ru dispersion. In situ NAP-XPS and computational results show that Nb-CeO2 maintains an electron-enriched Ru working state under reaction conditions, which is further promoted by illumination. Accordingly, 5 wt% Ru/Nb-CeO2 achieves an NH3 synthesis rate of 7.4 mmol g−1 h−1 at 350°C and 0.1 MPa and remains stable for 144 h. Kinetic analyses and in situ DRIFTS indicate that the electronically promoted Ru state alleviates N2-activation limitations and facilitates subsequent *NHx hydrogenation and NH3 desorption. Scale-up synthesis affords a 3 wt% Ru/Nb-CeO2-L catalyst stable for 480 h and operable under outdoor concentrated sunlight. A screening-level analysis estimates a catalyst-and-feedstock cost of 286–322 USD tNH3 −1 under the lower-bound electricity scenario, 42%–51% below the selected Cs-Ru/MgO benchmark within the same framework. These results identify lattice strain as a promising strategy for simultaneously stabilizing the oxygen sublattice and electronically promoting Ru for efficient solar-driven ammonia synthesis.

articles.title: Programmable Microgel Degradation in Dynamic Granular Hydrogels Guides Extracellular Matrix Assembly During Tissue Repair
articles.abstract: Granular hydrogels have attracted widespread interest for wound healing applications, yet their static design, in which microstructure and void space remain fixed, contrasts with the dynamic nature of tissue repair where processes like provisional extracellular matrix (pECM) assembly, cell organization, and nascent tissue formation evolve over time. Here, this disparity is addressed by designing dynamic granular hydrogels that are modularly assembled using microgels with pre‐programmed and precise degradation rates ranging from a few days to several weeks. Microgel degradation is controlled via modulation of hydrolytic susceptibility of hyaluronic acid polymers. The biological significance of timed pore expansion in dynamic granular hydrogels is investigated in a mouse muscle crush injury model. While slow‐degrading hydrogels support a distinct spatial assembly of cell‐instructive interstitial matrix and basement membrane proteins in the expanded pore space, this pECM remodeling is adversely altered in non‐degrading or fast‐degrading hydrogels. Slow‐degrading dynamic granular hydrogels also show long‐term therapeutic benefits on muscle wound healing, evidenced by reduced fibrosis, enhanced myogenesis, and improved functional force recovery. Collectively, these striking results demonstrate the profound significance of incorporating dynamicity through controlled microgel degradation in advanced granular biomaterials to improve tissue repair outcomes.

articles.title: Progressive Organization of Hydrogen‐Bonded Aramide Motifs via Foldamer–Macrocycle–Cage Architectures for Amplified Iodine Capture
articles.abstract: The rational design of high-performance adsorbents is central to environmental remediation and separation. Yet whether assembling identical adsorption-active motifs into higher-order architectures can amplify the contribution of each motif beyond simple additivity remains unclear. Herein, the same hydrogen-bonded aramide building block is progressively organized into acyclic foldamer, macrocycle, and cage architectures, establishing a motif-conserved platform for isolating architectural effects on iodine capture. Across the designed architecture series, uptake capacity, kinetics, and retention improve stepwise from the acyclic structures to the macrocycle and further to the cage. Normalization to the number of aramide motifs reveals that the adsorption contribution of each motif also increases along this sequence, demonstrating non-additive amplification rather than simple accumulation of binding sites. Notably, one cage captures up to 84 I3 − per molecule in the presence of a 100-fold excess of competing anions, representing the highest value reported for molecular adsorbents. Structural and computational analyses attribute this behavior primarily to strengthened motif-level host–guest interactions generated by progressive architectural organization, while solid-state packing modulates the distribution and accessibility of adsorption space. This work identifies progressive organization as a design paradigm for amplifying adsorption performance, offering insights into the development of advanced adsorbent materials.

articles.title: Supramolecular Stabilization of Wide‐Bandgap Perovskites Enables Durable Perovskite‐Organic Tandem Solar Cells
articles.abstract: Perovskite‐organic tandem solar cells (PO‐TSCs) offer a compelling platform for flexible photovoltaics by combining wide‐bandgap (WBG) perovskite top cells with mechanically compliant organic rear cells. However, their long‐term stability is critically limited by the intrinsic instability of WBG mixed‐halide perovskites. Here, through systematic ageing and mechanistic analyses, we identify halide phase segregation in the WBG perovskite sub‐cell under photothermal stress as the dominant degradation pathway that dictates the operational stability of the PO‐TSC investigated here. To address this challenge, we develop a halogenated cyclodextrin‐based supramolecular strategy that enables precise regulation of perovskite crystallization, defect passivation and halide distribution. Synergistic host‐guest, hydrogen‐bonding, halogen‐bonding and coordination interactions simultaneously regulate crystallization and suppress ion migration to result in stabilized halide homogeneity. Consequently, 1.80‐eV WBG devices achieve 20.60% efficiency with improved operational stability. Integrated PO‐TSCs deliver an efficiency of 27.17% (certified 26.3%) together with T80 lifetimes of 1100 h under maximum power point tracking (MPPT) operation and T85 lifetimes of 1128 h under thermal stress of 85°C, while flexible PO‐TSCs reach an efficiency of 24.00%. This work defines a general supramolecular design paradigm for efficient, durable and flexible tandem photovoltaics.

articles.title: Synthesis of Ti2B2Clx MBenes in Molten Salts From Theoretical and Experimental Perspectives
articles.abstract: The unique properties and application possibilities of two‐dimensional (2D) materials motivate the exploration of different nanolaminated compounds. Here, by using a molten salt approach, we selectively etch Ti2InB2 with ZnCl2 to produce a multilayer (ml) Ti2B2Clx MBene. Upon etching, indium atoms are completely removed from the precursor and replaced by chlorine surface terminations with a coverage of 1.1 < x < 1.4. Further, in situ x‐ray diffraction indicates a direct biphasic transformation from Ti2InB2 to ml‐MBene, with no signs of intermediate phase formation. A computational framework based on density functional theory further corroborates these experimental observations by showing a negative reaction free energy for the formation of ml‐MBene, favourable over all competing processes. In addition, A‐element substitution into the 3D Ti2ZnB2 phase is predicted to be endergonic, consistent with the absence of experimental evidence for its formation. Initial Li‐ion battery performance evaluation showed a stable discharge capacity similar to or better than MAX phases and other borides. Altogether, the theoretical framework combined with materials synthesis and characterization provides a general approach for 2D materials development, for further expansion of the family of 2D materials.

articles.title: Wafer‐Scale Direct Growth of Ultraclean Monolayer Amorphous Carbon on c‐Sapphire by Remote Catalytic Dehydrogenation
articles.abstract: Atomically thin amorphous carbon holds considerable promise for application in data storage, microelectronics, protective coatings, and flexible electronics. However, its device integration has been hindered by existing direct growth routes that rely on metal catalysts in contact with the substrate, causing metallic residue, film non‐uniformity, and the need for post‐growth processing. Here, we report the direct growth of monolayer amorphous carbon on a 2‐inch sapphire wafer via thermal chemical vapor deposition, in which a remotely positioned catalyst decomposes the carbon precursor into active carbon feedstock, keeping the growth substrate free of metallic contamination. X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy detects no catalyst residue across the wafer and confirms a highly sp2‐hybridized carbon network, while electron microscopy reveals a random polygonal carbon network lacking long‐range periodicity. Raman and atomic force microscopy mapping confirm uniform and atomically smooth monolayer coverage, while electrical measurements establish its insulating character with ambipolar, gate‐tunable hopping transport. This synthesis approach provides precise control over thickness and uniformity at the wafer scale, enabling direct device integration of amorphous carbon for a wide range of applications, particularly as an interlayer for epitaxial growth of freestanding semiconductor membranes.

articles.title: Where Ions Meet Electrons: Advanced Bioelectronic Interfaces With Organic Electrochemical Transistors
articles.abstract: Organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) have evolved from passive electrodes into active transducers that sense, amplify, and increasingly compute at the boundary between circuits and living tissue. Over the past decade, advances span molecular design of organic mixed ionic–electronic conductors (OMIECs), electrolyte and channel engineering, device architectures, and circuit integration, to system‐level translation. Unlike existing reviews that treat these in isolation, emphasizing single material classes, mechanisms, or applications, this article unifies them through bioelectronic interface design, working from biological demands to demonstrated capabilities. We analyze operating principles, benchmarking metrics and structure–property relationships across p‐type, n‐type, and biodegradable OMIECs. The electrolyte‐channel region emerges as where biology and electronics converge; we survey gel electrolytes, semiconducting hydrogels, and all‐gel devices, alongside planar, vertical, fiber, textile, and printed architectures. We assess how design choices impact performance across electrophysiological, biochemical, implantable, wearable, and plant‐bioelectronic applications, while addressing biocompatibility, stability, and standardization requirements. Finally, we outline OECT‐native platforms that consolidate sensing, memory, computation, and actuation within closed‐loop, autonomous bioelectronic interfaces, arguing that this convergence represents the most consequential near‐term direction for the field.

articles.title: “Activation‐Resistance Elimination” Regulation by Lanthanide/Transition Metal Ion‐Coordinated Nanostructures Intensifies Cuproptosis and Tumor Immunotherapy
articles.abstract: The therapeutic efficacy of cuproptosis is constrained by its insufficient activation and resistance mechanisms. Here, a lanthanide/transition metal ion‐coordinated nanoparticle, La‐Cu@Lap/IWR‐1, with optimized coordination, has been proven to achieve remarkable results in realizing comprehensive resistance‐eliminating cuproptosis activation. La3+ not only enhances Cu2+‐mediated multiple enzyme‐mimetic activities via coordination to amplify oxidative stress but also disrupts lysosomal acidification to improve copper ion availability. Moreover, combined with lapatinib (Lap), it alleviates the shielding effect of mediator of cell motility 1 (MEMO1) on Cu2+, significantly strengthening the cuproptosis activation efficacy. Meanwhile, the released Wnt inhibitor IWR‐1 can not only inhibit the Wnt/β‐catenin signaling pathway that is concomitantly activated during cuproptosis induction to weaken the oxidative stress tolerance of tumor cells but also synergize with Lap to downregulate hypoxia‐inducible factor 1α (HIF‐1α) expression, thereby effectively eliminating cuproptosis resistance. This comprehensive cuproptosis not only triggers significant immunogenic cell death but also synchronously inhibits key steps of tumor metastasis, such as epithelial‐mesenchymal transition and extracellular matrix remodeling.
